extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys) preparing or evaluating 37 CFR 1.131/1.132 affidavits and related evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing, evaluating, and using affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (and related provisions) to antedate references, including what must be shown, who may sign, required evidence, and special rules for genus/species and common-owner references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-authorship (overcoming reference by co-authored publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant is one of the co-authors of a publication cited against his or her application, he or she may overcome the rejection by filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131. Alternatively, the applicant may overcome the rejection by filing a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 establishing that the article is describing applicant’s own work. An affidavit or declaration by applicant alone indicating that applicant is the sole inventor and that the others were merely working under his or her direction is sufficient to remove the publication as a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Katz. Use 1.132 when showing the article describes applicant’s own invention. An affidavit by applicant alone claiming sole inventorship and that others worked under direction can remove the publication as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (evidence that a third-party reference derived from applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the unclaimed subject matter of a patent, application publication, or other publication is applicant’s own invention, a rejection (which is not a statutory bar) on that patent or publication may be removed by submission of evidence establishing the fact that the patentee, applicant of the published application, or author derived his or her knowledge of the relevant subject matter from applicant. Moreover applicant must further show that he or she made the invention upon which the relevant disclosure ... is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Mathews and In re Facius. Evidence must establish derivation from applicant and that applicant actually made the invention underlying the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities applied against the claims (when non-statutory activities can be antedated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is a statutory bar, a rejection based on an activity showing that the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date of the application may be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the date of the activity. Alternatively, the applicant(s) may overcome the rejection by filing a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the applicant(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish statutory bars (which cannot be antedated) from activities that can be antedated via 1.131 or shown to have been performed by applicant under 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much of the claimed invention must be shown (commensurateness / species/genus rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit or declaration must establish possession of either the whole invention claimed or something falling within the claim (such as a species of a claimed genus), in the sense that the claim as a whole reads on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Tanczyn — showing part of a claimed alloy (nitrogen only) is insufficient if claim requires both nitrogen and molybdenum. Where differences between claim and reference are small (rendering claim obvious), 1.131 may need to show no more than the reference. If affidavit not identical to reference but shows completion commensurate with claimed invention it's sufficient (In re Wakefield). If affidavit not fully commensurate, applicant can still overcome rejection by showing differences would have been obvious in view of applicant's 1.131 evidence — but affidavit must establish possession of the basic inventive concept (In re Spiller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Swearing behind combined references (showing completion prior to any combined ref date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on a combination of references by showing completion of the invention by applicant prior to the effective date of any of the references; applicant need not antedate the reference with the earliest filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit must show possession of the whole invention or something within the claims prior to the effective date of the reference being antedated. Applicant may rely on teachings of a secondary reference to show that differences would have been obvious, but the affidavit must still establish possession of the claimed invention, not just what Reference A shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule as to generic claims (single species can antedate genus in most cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing completion of the invention of only a single species, within the genus, prior to the effective date of the reference or activity (assuming the reference/activity is not a statutory bar or a patent/application publication claiming the same invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Biesecker; exceptions and special practice apply in unpredictable arts (see MPEP §715.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species and predictability (when single-species showing is insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where generic claims have been rejected on a reference or activity which discloses a species not antedated by the affidavit or declaration, the rejection will not ordinarily be withdrawn ... unless the applicant is able to establish that he or she was in possession of the generic invention prior to the effective date of the reference or activity. In other words, the affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If predictability is in question (unpredictable arts), showing one or a few species generally not sufficient. The affidavit must provide an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability. Size of genus affects how many species may be needed (e.g., small genus may need fewer species demonstrated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claim: overcoming when reference discloses the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131 directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by a showing of prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Spiller and related cases. Indirect antedating requires showing obviousness relationship between species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim: handling references that disclose species or several species
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of a species in a cited reference is sufficient to prevent a later applicant from obtaining a 'generic claim.' Where the only pertinent disclosure in the reference or activity is a single species of the claimed genus, the applicant can overcome the rejection directly under 37 CFR 1.131 by showing prior possession of the species disclosed. A reference which discloses several species of a claimed genus can be overcome directly under 37 CFR 1.131 only by a showing that the applicant completed, prior to the date of the reference or activity, all of the species shown in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant cannot show possession of the species of the reference, applicant may attempt to antedate indirectly by showing possession of one or more species that provide an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability (test: would facts persuade one skilled in art that applicant possessed as much of the invention as shown in the reference). Cases: In re Stempel, In re Plumb, In re Clarke, In re Hostettler, In re Rainer, In re Shokal, In re Schaub.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species versus embodiments (difference between species of a genus and multiple embodiments of same invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: References or activities which disclose one or more embodiments of a single claimed invention, as opposed to species of a claimed genus, can be overcome by filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit showing prior completion of a single embodiment of the invention, whether it is the same or a different embodiment from that disclosed in the reference or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Fong and In re Defano. Distinguish 'species of a genus' versus 'different embodiments of the same invention' when assessing sufficiency of 1.131 evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference discloses claimed genus (single species generally sufficient except unpredictable arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the reference or activity discloses the claimed genus, a showing of completion of a single species within the genus is sufficient to antedate the reference or activity under 37 CFR 1.131.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts, showing one or few species is generally not sufficient. The test is whether species completed by applicant provide adequate basis for inferring the invention has generic applicability. Number of species required scales with genus size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make an affidavit or declaration (qualified signatories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following parties may make an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131: (A) All the inventors of the subject matter claimed. (B) An affidavit or declaration by less than all named inventors is accepted where it is shown that less than all named inventors invented the subject matter of the claim(s) under rejection. (C) If a petition under 37 CFR 1.47 was granted or the application was accepted under 37 CFR 1.42 or 1.43, the affidavit or declaration may be signed by the 1.47 applicant or the legal representative, where appropriate. (D) The assignee or other party in interest when it is not possible to produce the affidavit or declaration of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits to overcome rejections must be made by inventor(s), a party qualified under 1.42/1.43/1.47, or assignee/party in interest when inventor unavailable (cites Ex parte Foster). If one named inventor is unavailable, remaining joint inventors may sign provided a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of signature is filed with proof of unavailability (see MPEP §409.03(d)). Petitions under 1.183 decided by Office of Petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit is a statement in writing made under oath before a notary public, magistrate, or officer authorized to administer oaths. 37 CFR 1.68 permits a declaration to be used instead of an affidavit. The declaration must include an acknowledgment by the declarant that willful false statements ... are punishable by fine or imprisonment (18 U.S.C. 1001) and may jeopardize the validity of the application or any patent issuing thereon. The declarant must set forth that all statements made of the declarant’s own knowledge are true and that all statements made on information and belief are believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §604-604.06 for additional information on formal affidavit requirements. Declarations per 1.68 are allowed in lieu of sworn affidavits but must include the statutory warning/acknowledgment and knowledge/belief language.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention (limitations on using 1.131)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference is a noncommonly owned U.S. application or publication claiming the same invention as applicant and its publication date is less than 1 year prior to the presentation of claims to that invention in the application being examined, applicant’s remedy, if any, must be by way of 37 CFR 41.202 instead of 37 CFR 1.131. If the reference is a U.S. patent which claims the same invention as the application and its issue date is more than 1 year prior to the presentation of claims to that invention in the application, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference is a U.S. application publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b), or a WIPO publication claiming the same invention and its publication date is more than 1 year prior to presentation of claims, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(2) should be made only if the application being examined was filed after the publication date of the reference. Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 as appropriate. Note complexity when references are commonly owned or when interference practice applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership and terminal disclaimer/1.130 practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the reference and the application (or patent under reexamination) are commonly owned, and the inventions defined by the claims ... are not identical but are not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or application publication not only where there is verbatim correspondence between claims but also where there is no patentable distinction between respective claims (various cases cited). If claims are identical or not patentably distinct, the application and patent are claiming the 'same patentable invention' and interference rules apply (37 CFR 41.203(a)). See MPEP §718 for terminal disclaimer practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts and documentary evidence required (must show facts, not conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential thing to be shown under 37 CFR 1.131 is priority of invention and this may be done by any satisfactory evidence of the fact. FACTS, not conclusions, must be alleged. Evidence in the form of exhibits may accompany the affidavit or declaration. Each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in the affidavit or declaration, in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable exhibits include: attached sketches; blueprints; photographs; reproductions of notebook entries; an accompanying model; supporting witness statements; testimony given in an interference; disclosure documents. Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91. A general allegation of prior completion is insufficient. Original exhibits or photocopies must accompany affidavit or absence satisfactorily explained per 1.131(b) (Donovan). Examiner must consider entire evidence package; an exhibit need not support all claim limitations if declaration supports missing ones. Vague/general descriptions of exhibits amount to mere pleading and are insufficient (In re Borkowski). Applicant must clearly explain which facts the exhibits establish and rely upon (In re Harry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of dates (how dates can be alleged and when actual dates needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the dates of the exhibits have been removed or blocked off, the matter of dates can be taken care of in the body of the oath or declaration. When alleging that conception or a reduction to practice occurred prior to the effective date of the reference, the dates in the oath or declaration may be the actual dates or, if the applicant does not desire to disclose actual dates, he or she may merely allege that the acts occurred prior to a specified date. However, the actual dates of acts relied on to establish diligence must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the body of the affidavit/declaration to explain or specify dates when originals lack visible dates; provide actual dates for diligence periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways to show prior invention under 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131(b) provides three ways in which an applicant can establish prior invention of the claimed subject matter: (A) actual reduction to practice of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference; or (B) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to a subsequent (actual) reduction to practice; or (C) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to the filing date of the application (constructive reduction to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there has not been reduction to practice prior to the reference, applicant must show diligence in completion from just prior to the reference continuously up to the date of actual reduction to practice or filing (filing = constructive reduction to practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception and reduction to practice standards (what constitutes each)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the mental part of the inventive act, but it must be capable of proof (e.g., by drawings, complete disclosure to another person). In general, proof of actual reduction to practice requires showing that the apparatus actually existed and worked for its intended purpose, though some devices are so simple mere construction suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mergenthaler v. Scudder, In re Asahi/America, Newkirk v. Lulejian, Sachs v. Wadsworth. Photographs coupled with articles and a technical report can be sufficient. Emphasize that conception alone confers no rights unless followed by reasonable diligence and reduction or filing (Automatic Weighing Mach. Co. v. Pneumatic Scale Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between interference practice and 1.131 practice
rubrics_metrics.description: For the most part, the terms 'conception,' 'reasonable diligence,' and 'reduction to practice' have the same meanings under 37 CFR 1.131 as in interference proceedings. However, the purpose of filing a 1.131 affidavit is to antedate the effective date of a reference, not to demonstrate prior invention per se, and the 'conception' and 'reduction to practice' required under the rule need not be the same as in the interference sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences: in interference practice, reduction to practice requires proof that a utility was known, whereas under 1.131 proof of utility is required only if the reference discloses a utility. Whether test results are required depends on facts. Interference practice requires corroboration of conception/diligence/reduction, whereas 1.131 affidavits/averments do not require corroboration and an applicant may stand on his/her own affidavit (Ex parte Hook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (what must be shown and when it matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conception occurs prior to the date of the reference, but reduction to practice is afterward, it is not enough merely to allege that applicant had been diligent; applicant must show evidence of facts establishing diligence. In determining sufficiency of a 1.131 affidavit or declaration, diligence need not be considered unless conception prior to the effective date is clearly established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence comes into play only after prior conception is established; applicant must present factual evidence of continuous diligence from just prior to the reference date up to reduction to practice or filing. See Ex parte Hunter and Ex parte Kantor.
